Q: How do I make git commit -a not add submodule changes? A:

The short answer is that git commit -a is designed to stage all tracked files that have changed in the working tree, and in Git's eyes, a submodule is just a tracked pointer (a gitlink) to a specific commit. If your working tree's submodule is at a different commit than the index, -a will include it.

Here are the best ways to solve this, ranging from configuration changes to workflow adjustments.

1. The Configuration Fix: ignore = dirty

You can tell Git to ignore changes to submodules during normal operations by modifying your .gitmodules file or your local .git/config.

Add ignore = dirty to the submodule configuration. This ensures that changes to the submodule's contents or its current HEAD pointer are not automatically picked up by commands like git status or git commit -a.

In your .gitmodules file:

[submodule "my-submodule"]
    path = my-submodule
    url = https://github.com/user/repo.git
    ignore = all
  • ignore = dirty: Ignores changes to the submodule working tree, but will still show if the submodule is at a different commit.
  • ignore = all: Ignores the submodule entirely during git commit -a. You would have to explicitly git add the submodule to update its pointer.

2. The "Better Habit" Fix: Avoid -a

The most reliable way to prevent accidental reverts is to stop using the -a (all) flag. Instead, stage specific files or directories:

git add src/
git commit -m "My specific changes"

If you prefer the speed of -a, you can use the interactive staging tool to review exactly what is being committed:

git commit -p

This allows you to "y" (yes) or "n" (no) each hunk of code, including the submodule pointer change.

3. The Automation Fix: Use a pre-commit Hook

If "Programmer B" is the problem, you can enforce a check on their local machine. Create a script in .git/hooks/pre-commit that aborts the commit if a submodule is staged but shouldn't be.

Example pre-commit snippet:

#!/bin/sh
# Check if any submodules are staged for commit
if git diff --cached --submodule | grep -q '^Submodule'; then
  echo "Error: You are attempting to commit a submodule change."
  echo "If this was accidental (due to git commit -a), please unstage it."
  exit 1
fi

4. The Workflow Fix: Automatic Updates

The reason this happens is usually that the developer forgot to update their submodules after a pull/rebase. You can automate this globally so it's harder to forget:

git config --global submodule.recurse true

With this enabled, commands like git checkout, git pull, and git rebase will attempt to update submodules to the expected commits automatically, keeping the working tree in sync with the index.

Summary

Method Pros Cons
ignore = all Completely prevents -a from touching submodules. You might forget to intentionally update the submodule later.
submodule.recurse Keeps the environment in sync automatically. Can be slow on very large projects.
pre-commit hook Catches the error before the commit is made. Each developer must install/enable it locally.
Avoid -a Best practice for clean history. Requires changing muscle memory.
